source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Laird's main text names three impasse types: state no-change, operator tie/conflict, operator no-change. Only the glossary says there are technically four (state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict). Constraint-failure does not appear in this paper.
numbers: Section 3: 3 types. Glossary: 4 types. Constraint-failure: 0 mentions. Soar version 9.6.
quote: There are three types of impasses that correspond to the different types of failures of the decision procedure
limits: The count of types differs by source, so there is no single canonical list.
agent_relevance: Define our S6 triggers by what our code can detect (no candidate, tied candidates, contradicting verdicts, no state change), not by copying Soar names.

source: Soar manual, chapter The Soar Architecture (online)
finding: The manual's contents list four impasse types: tie, conflict, constraint-failure, no-change. Its overview paragraph on the same page says there are three possible impasses. The manual disagrees with itself.
numbers: Contents: 4 types. Overview paragraph: 3 types.
limits: The page text I obtained did not include the detailed impasse section, so the definition of constraint-failure is not verified from the manual.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on constraint-failure as established until a source with its definition is opened. Working guess only: required and prohibit preferences leave no legal operator.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR
finding: The NL2GenSym critic output lists five impasse types: state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict, constraint-failure. It also reports that generated rules fell into an infinite loop from a state no-change impasse and advises explicit handlers for all five.
numbers: Run cap 500,000 decision cycles, then counted as failure. Rules needing more than 10 minimum cycles were prone to loops.
limits: Anecdotal critic text. No counts of which impasse types occurred.
agent_relevance: A no-change loop is the common failure of LLM-written control. Keep a hard cycle cap plus a no-change detector.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: An impasse is detected by a fixed rule in the decision procedure, not by the system judging itself. Tie or conflict means preferences are insufficient or contradictory. Operator no-change means the same operator stays selected across two or more decisions.
numbers: Operator no-change threshold: the same operator is still selected in the next selection phase.
limits: Operator no-change also fires when an action simply takes several cycles in the world. Laird says the right answer then is to wait. A bare repeat counter would give false alarms.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and a code-checked no-change detector, with an exemption for slow but progressing steps.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: A substate has its own preference memory and uses the same decision procedure. It can read the superstate but passes back only results. Non-result substate data is deleted when the impasse is resolved. The impasse ends as soon as the superstate can decide, even if substate reasoning is unfinished.
numbers: One substate per state; substates nest in a stack. Elaboration results persist only while their supporting superstate structure exists. Results of an applied operator do not retract.
limits: Described, not tested against alternatives.
agent_relevance: Matches our subgoal-returns-only-its-result rule. Add: end the subgoal the moment the parent can decide, and drop scratch text.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Laird says time in a substate can be monitored so a non-optimal or even random decision is made when time is short. Deliberate substate reasoning costs more time than rule firing.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Design statement, not measured.
agent_relevance: Supports G6 (never abstain): give every subgoal a budget and a default pick when it runs out.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Laird states that additional preferences can always eliminate an operator-selection impasse; in the extreme this means creating copies of tied operators. So tie and conflict impasses can always be ended by a decision. State no-change and operator no-change carry no such guarantee.
numbers: Footnote 4.
limits: A claim about the design, not a test on real agents.
agent_relevance: Our tie handler can always end by picking and logging the pick. Only the no-candidate case needs new operator generation.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Laird maps Soar levels to deliberation: rules and retrieval are the fast level, substate processing is the deliberate metalevel, and chunking moves behaviour down a level with experience. He calls the mapping to Kahneman System 1 and 2 natural but one possible mapping.
numbers: Text only, no data.
limits: The author hedges; no test that substate use tracks human effort.
agent_relevance: Weak support for escalating from cheap to costly reasoning on impasse. Do not cite it as human evidence.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR
finding: An LLM generator writes Soar rules for the Water Jug task and a critic LLM revises them from real Soar run output. Success at producing working rules was 86 percent (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and 91 percent (Qwen-max). Zero-shot success was 0 percent. One-shot with an example was 55 percent (Gemini 2.5 Pro) and 66 percent (Qwen-max).
numbers: N=100 cases: 25 easy, 25 medium, 30 hard, 20 three-jug. Average decision cycles 1.76 times optimum (Gemini) and 1.98 times (Qwen).
limits: One toy task, one lab, no impasse-specific measurement. The LLM writes the rules; Soar does not call the LLM at an impasse.
agent_relevance: An LLM cannot write Soar control knowledge zero-shot but can with an execution-grounded critic. Fits G2.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR
finding: Hand-written basic Soar rules with no search control solved most Water Jug cases but wandered. Average decision cycles were about 3390 times the optimum overall and about 11507 times on hard cases. Success on hard cases was 46.67 percent.
numbers: Manual baseline: success 84 percent; Avg.DC 27018.94 against Avg.Min.DC 7.97. Hard: 147984.64 against 12.86.
limits: Manual rules were deliberately basic. This is a floor, not a fair expert baseline.
agent_relevance: Shows what unresolved ties cost: search thousands of times longer than needed. Supports spending effort on tie resolution.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR
finding: Ablation: removing the critic loop cut success by 23 points overall and 37 points on hard and three-jug cases, and cycles rose above 1000 times the minimum. Removing the basic knowledge base cut success 17 points; removing the case memory cut it 14 points. A smaller model (Flash) with the framework beat a larger one (Pro) used one-shot.
numbers: Success drops in points on 100 cases: critic -23, knowledge base -17, case base -14. Flash with framework 86 percent against Pro one-shot 55 percent.
limits: Single run per condition as reported, no intervals. The authors call the model-size inversion preliminary. The authors built the framework, so this is not independent.
agent_relevance: The execution-grounded critic mattered most. Supports G2 and G3: checks that run, not model opinion.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: STARS is a Soar agent that widens the LLM's candidate answers (search tree), analyses them in the agent, repairs bad ones, then selects. Without human oversight, task completion rose from 52.5, 66.7, 35.7 percent (prompt-only baseline) to 77.5, 94.4, 92.9 percent on kitchen, groceries, office tasks.
numbers: Three simulated robot tasks with 35, 15, 12 objects. GPT-3 for tree and repair, GPT-4 for selection. 10 runs per task; SD 2.04, 1.76, 2.26 points. With human oversight both reached 100 percent.
limits: Simulation only, one scripted user, one repair attempt per response. Not an impasse test: STARS is a pipeline inside a Soar agent.
agent_relevance: Strongest measured result for agent-side checking of LLM proposals. Analysis and repair did the work, not wider sampling.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: Ablation shows which stage mattered. Search tree alone did not help (kitchen 50.0, office 21.4 against baseline 52.5, 35.7). Adding analysis and repair gave large gains (+27.5, +11.1, +42.9 points over tree-only). Adding model selection helped groceries and office (+16.6, +28.6) but not kitchen (0). Tree plus selection without repair was worse than tree alone on kitchen (40.0 against 50.0).
numbers: Kitchen/groceries/office completion: ST 50.0/66.7/21.4; STS 40.0/66.7/21.4; STAR 77.5/77.8/64.3; STARS 77.5/94.4/92.9.
limits: Authors blame the kitchen selection failure on missing task context. GPT-4 selector showed a small recency bias. One reported run per condition.
agent_relevance: A model choosing among tied options is unreliable without a repair step first. Supports G5. Test any model selector per task.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: STARS used several times the tokens of the baseline. Over 70 percent of kitchen responses, 58 percent of groceries and 85 percent of office responses from the LLM were unviable.
numbers: Tokens, baseline vs STARS: kitchen 41,407 vs 139,871; groceries 17,078 vs 61,808; office 12,992 vs 76,056 (about 3.4x, 3.6x, 5.9x).
limits: No equal-token control such as plain best-of-N at the same cost, so the gain is not shown to beat sampling at equal budget.
agent_relevance: G7 applies: compare any STARS-like loop with plain sampling at the same tokens before adopting it.

source: CogRec (2025) Soar plus LLM for explainable recommendation, arXiv 2512.24113
finding: On an impasse the Soar agent sends its state to Deepseek-V3. The reply becomes a chunk, so later LLM calls fall. Gain over the best baseline (GPT4Rec) is 4.1 to 9.1 percent relative across three datasets. MovieLens-1M HR@10 is 0.3124 against 0.2956 (GPT4Rec) and 0.2901 (LLM-Direct).
numbers: ML-1M 6,040 users; Amazon Movies 123,960; Yelp 43,702. Soar with about 20 hand rules: HR@10 0.0511 on ML-1M. Gain over plain LLM on ML-1M about 7.7 percent relative.
limits: No significance tests, no cost numbers, one LLM, ablations only in figures, impasse detection not formalised, tables look rounded. I read it through a page-fetch summary, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Gain over a plain LLM is small. Weak evidence that impasse routing helps. Do not cite as proof.

source: CogRec (2025) Soar plus LLM for explainable recommendation, arXiv 2512.24113
finding: Ablations are reported only as figures. Without chunking, performance fell toward the plain LLM and call frequency stayed high. Without LLM bootstrap it dropped sharply. No numbers are given.
numbers: No numeric values for ablations. Soar baseline uses about 20 rules, the no-bootstrap variant 5.
limits: Inconsistent baselines, figures only, one case study for the explainability claim.
agent_relevance: Gap: nobody has a clean effect size for LLM-at-impasse against LLM-always. We should measure it ourselves.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: ToT is the closest LLM analogue of a tie impasse: propose several thoughts, have the model evaluate each, search with backtracking. On Game of 24 with GPT-4: input-output 7.3 percent, chain of thought 4.0, CoT self-consistency (k=100) 9.0, ToT breadth 1 gave 45, ToT breadth 5 gave 74.
numbers: 100 games (indices 901-1000). Best of 100 CoT samples reached 49 percent. Cost: ToT about 5.5k completion tokens per case against 6.7k for 100 CoT trials.
limits: One model, three tasks chosen so that search helps. Authors say ToT may be unnecessary where GPT-4 already does well.
agent_relevance: Propose, evaluate, backtrack beat sampling at similar tokens on a search-shaped task. Use tie-style branching only where branches exist.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: On Mini Crosswords ToT reached 60 percent word-level success and solved 4 of 20 games. IO and CoT stayed under 16 percent word-level. Removing backtracking dropped word success to 20 percent. Removing pruning gave worse results. With an oracle best-state output ToT solved 7 of 20.
numbers: N=20 games. In Game of 24 around 60 percent of CoT samples failed after the first step.
limits: The model's own state evaluator sometimes pruned correct words. 20 games is small.
agent_relevance: Backtracking and a fall-back path mattered more than the model evaluator. The evaluator is a weak link, which supports code-side selection (G5).

source: Chain-in-Tree study (2025) Back to Sequential Reasoning in LLM Tree Search, arXiv 2509.25835
finding: Tree search is expensive and much branching is wasted on trivial steps. A rule that decides when branching is needed cut tokens, calls and runtime by 75 to 85 percent with small accuracy change (GSM8K 0.98 to 0.97, Math500 0.87 to 0.86 on Qwen3-32B).
numbers: 100 test items per benchmark, 14 settings. Time saving 77.3 and 78.2 percent. With a weak evaluator (LLaMA3-8B) accuracy fell toward chain-of-thought (0.27 against 0.39 on Math500).
limits: Math only, 100 items each, 4 of 14 settings were unstable for one variant. Read through a page-fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Supports branch only on a signal (G1): a tie trigger is cheaper than always branching. A weak model as the branch decider breaks it.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking the model to review and fix its own answer with no outside feedback did not help and often hurt. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: 95.5 to 89.0, 82.0 to 80.0, 49.0 to 43.0.
numbers: Three benchmarks, two models. Multi-agent debate at 9 responses scored 83.0 on GSM8K against 88.2 for self-consistency.
limits: Earlier reported gains used oracle labels to stop. External feedback such as code execution does help. Numbers read through a page-fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: resolving a conflict impasse by asking the model to reconsider fails. Resolve with real output or a check.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA describes Soar's impasse in two sentences: if no action is valid or several tie, an impasse occurs and Soar creates a subgoal. It gives no impasse mechanism for language agents. Its decision loop is propose, evaluate, select, execute, with selection by argmax, softmax or majority vote, or rejecting all and looping back to propose.
numbers: Conceptual paper; no experiments of its own.
limits: It maps Soar parts to agents but does not test impasse-driven control. Its own future-work list asks for metareasoning to decide how much to think.
agent_relevance: CoALA's reject-all-and-loop-back is a no-candidate impasse by another name. No evidence from CoALA either way on impasse routing.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA notes most language agents still only propose a single action, and that only recent work does iterative propose and evaluate (ToT, RAP). It lists metareasoning, to estimate whether planning pays, as open.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Position paper, TMLR 2024.
agent_relevance: Marks adaptive stopping as an open problem, so our impasse-triggered deliberation is not covered by published evidence.

source: Joshi and Ustun (2023) Augmenting Cognitive Architectures with Large Language Models
finding: A proposal paper: a Soar or Sigma impasse opens a substate whose goal is to query the LLM, with learned soft-token operator embeddings, and chunking turns the answer into a rule that prevents the impasse. It argues the architecture should choose the final action rather than the LLM, as STARS did.
numbers: 0 experiments, 0 numbers.
limits: Sigma lacks chunking and operator embeddings, so the scheme is not built.
agent_relevance: An untested pattern. See STARS and CogRec for measured versions.

source: Lehman, Lewis, Newell (1991) Integrating Knowledge Sources in Language Comprehension (NL-Soar)
finding: NL-Soar is an early model where impasses on a comprehend operator open subgoals in language, semantics and constraint spaces, and chunking turns the search into recognition. A snip operator repairs wrong earlier choices. It targets 200 to 300 words per minute.
numbers: Grammar coverage about 75 percent of Allen's basic English grammar. No accuracy or timing data.
limits: A model with no human data fit in this paper. Garden-path predictions were still under study.
agent_relevance: The impasse, subgoal, chunk loop works as a design but gives no effect size here.

source: Brown and VanLehn (1980) Repair Theory: a generative theory of bugs in procedural skills
finding: Seen only in search summaries. Students with an incomplete procedure hit an impasse and apply a repair; different repairs at the same impasse give different bugs. The theory was checked against a large database of multidigit subtraction bugs.
numbers: Counts not obtained.
limits: A secondary summary says the evidence base is mainly primary-school arithmetic. PDF fetch failed, so no numbers verified.
agent_relevance: Human-side support for impasse then repair. Must open the paper before citing numbers.

source: Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness
finding: Seen only in the abstract summary. Chunking can cut the number of steps while making total run time worse, because some learned rules are costly to match. This is a boundary condition on learning from impasses.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Abstract-level only. Doorenbos, Tambe, Newell 1992 (Learning 10,000 chunks) was found by title only.
agent_relevance: Rule-style subgoal libraries can slow the agent. A stored helper needs a retrieval cost limit. Overlaps the chunking subfield.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom (2017) A Standard Model of the Mind
finding: Seen only in search summaries. The model came from mapping ACT-R, Sigma and Soar, reflects consensus not unanimity, and critics say its evidence standard for convergence is weak. Whether impasse-driven subgoaling is in the shared core was not confirmed.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Rival view: ACT-R does not use impasses as its main control device; not verified here.
agent_relevance: Impasse subgoaling may be a Soar-specific choice, not a field consensus. Check before calling it established.
